content: All findings from the Declaration of Interest (DOI) statements submitted by experts were handled in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) DOI guidelines. Each case was reviewed individually, and the outcomes were communicated to the respective experts. The management of declared conflicts of interest followed the WHO guidelines for declaration of interests by experts. If a conflict of interest was deemed insignificant and unlikely to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility, the experts were only required to disclose the conflict openly at the beginning of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting, with no further actions taken. However, conflicts of interest that required action by WHO staff arose when experts had received funding from an organization or institution to conduct primary research or had performed a systematic review directly related to any of the guideline recommendations. In such cases, the concerned experts were restricted from participating in discussions or formulating recommendations during the GDG meeting. The WHO recommendations for the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections were developed through a rigorous process. This included 24 systematic reviews summarized in 57 GRADE tables, which provided the evidence base for the recommendations. The technical consultation process was structured to allow participants to discuss each recommendation drafted by the WHO Steering Group. Revisions were made as necessary through group discussions, and final adoption of recommendations was achieved by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, provided that those who disagreed did not strongly oppose the decision. In cases of strong disagreement, the dissent would have been recorded, although no such disagreements were noted during the consultation. If consensus could not be reached, the disputed recommendation or decision was put to a vote. Voting was conducted by a show of hands among GDG members, and a simple majority (more than half of the participants) was required for a recommendation to stand, except in cases involving safety concerns. In such instances, the WHO Secretariat would decide not to issue a recommendation. WHO staff, external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading, and observers were not eligible to vote. If the issue to be voted on involved primary research or systematic reviews conducted by participants with declared academic conflicts of interest, those participants could join the discussion but were not allowed to vote. In addition to evaluating the scientific evidence and its quality, the GDG considered values, preferences, applicability issues, and costs when formulating the final recommendations. The strength of each recommendation was determined based on the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits versus harms, values and preferences, and resource implications. Strong recommendations were based on evidence of moderate to high quality, while conditional recommendations were based on evidence of low to very low quality. Evidence-to-decision tables were used to document and synthesize these considerations and to record the rationale for any changes made to the default strength of the recommendations. Before the technical consultation, the WHO Steering Group prepared a draft version of evidence summaries and corresponding recommendations. This draft was shared with participants two weeks before the meeting for their comments. During the meeting, the draft recommendations were modified based on participants' deliberations and feedback. After the meeting, the Steering Group revised the full guideline document to reflect the participants' discussions and decisions accurately. The draft guideline was then sent electronically to GDG members for further comments before being submitted to the External Review Group for peer review. The Steering Group carefully evaluated the peer reviewers' inputs for inclusion in the guideline document. Post-consultation modifications were limited to correcting factual errors and improving language clarity. The final revised version was sent electronically to the technical consultation participants for their final approval. The overarching principles guiding the recommendations were based on consensus and aligned with good clinical practice principles. These principles emphasized the importance of improving care related to the prevention and treatment of infectious morbidities around childbirth. They also highlighted fundamental and cross-cutting issues relevant to the prioritized questions in the guideline. These principles are expected to guide end-users in adapting and implementing the guideline across various contexts and settings. Standard infection prevention and control measures should be observed in maternity care to optimize the effects of the recommended interventions. As part of global efforts to reduce antimicrobial resistance, antibiotics should only be administered when there is a clear medical indication, as recommended in the guideline, and when the expected benefits outweigh potential harms within the local context. Hospitals should establish committees to monitor antimicrobial usage, provide feedback to prescribers, and regularly update antimicrobial formularies. Prophylactic and therapeutic use of antibiotics should be informed by the narrowest antibacterial spectrum, the woman’s medical history, the simplest effective dose, cost-effectiveness, and local susceptibility patterns. Bacterial culture samples should be obtained before initiating antibiotic therapy, but this should not delay prompt administration of antibiotics. The WHO technical consultation adopted 20 recommendations addressing prioritized questions related to the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections. These included recommendations on practices such as perineal/pubic shaving, the use of antiseptic agents for vaginal and cesarean births, and antibiotic prophylaxis for infection-prone conditions and obstetric procedures. When evidence of effectiveness was available, the comparative safety and efficacy of different antibiotic classes or regimens were considered to issue additional recommendations. The recommendations for treating maternal peripartum infections specifically addressed antibiotic management of chorioamnionitis and postpartum endometritis. The quality of supporting evidence was rated as very low, low, moderate, or high, and the strength of each recommendation was assessed as strong or conditional. To ensure proper understanding and implementation of each recommendation, additional remarks summarizing the GDG discussions were included where necessary. For example, routine perineal/pubic shaving before vaginal birth is not recommended, as there is no evidence of clinical benefit, and the quality of evidence is very low. Potential complications of shaving, such as irritation, redness, and discomfort, outweigh any perceived benefits. The decision regarding shaving should be left to the woman and not imposed by healthcare providers.
